verses.zh: 论大马士革的默示：看哪，大马士革已被废弃，不再为城，必变作乱堆。
verses.en: This is an oracle[NOTE:1] about Damascus:“Look, Damascus is no longer a city,it is a heap of ruins!
notes: See note at Isa 13:1.

verses.zh: 亚罗珥的城邑已被撇弃，必成为牧羊之处；羊在那里躺卧，无人惊吓。
verses.en: The cities of Aroer are abandoned.[NOTE:1] They will be used for herds,which will lie down there in peace.[NOTE:2]
notes: Three cities are known by this name in the OT: (1) an Aroer located near the Arnon, (2) an Aroer in Ammon, and (3) an Aroer of Judah. (See BDB 792-93 s.v. עֲרֹעֵר, and HALOT 883 s.v. II עֲרוֹעֵר.) There is no mention of an Aroer in Syrian territory. For this reason some want to emend the text here to עֲזֻבוֹת עָרַיהָ עֲדֵי עַד (ʿazuvot ʿarayha ʿade ʿad, “her cities are permanently abandoned”). However, Aroer near the Arnon was taken by Israel and later conquered by the Syrians. (See Josh 12:2; 13:9, 16; Judg 11:26; 2 Kgs 10:33). This oracle pertains to Israel as well as Syria (note v. 3), so it is possible that this is a reference to Israelite and/or Syrian losses in Transjordan.
Heb “and they lie down, and there is no one scaring [them].”

verses.zh: 以法莲不再有保障；大马士革不再有国权；亚兰所剩下的必像以色列人的荣耀消灭一样。这是万军之耶和华说的。
verses.en: Fortified cities will disappear from Ephraim,and Damascus will lose its kingdom.[NOTE:1] The survivors in Syriawill end up like the splendor of the Israelites,”says the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.
notes: Heb “and kingship from Damascus”; cf. NASB “And sovereignty from Damascus.”

verses.zh: 到那日，雅各的荣耀必至枵薄；他肥胖的身体必渐瘦弱。
verses.en: “At that time[NOTE:1] Jacob’s splendor will be greatly diminished,[NOTE:2] and he will become skin and bones.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “in that day” (so KJV). The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “will be tiny.”
Heb “and the fatness of his flesh will be made lean.”

verses.zh: 就必像收割的人收敛禾稼，用手割取穗子，又像人在利乏音谷拾取遗落的穗子。
verses.en: It will be as when one gathers the grain harvest and his hand gleans the ear of grain.It will be like one gathering the ears of grainin the Valley of Rephaim.

verses.zh: 其间所剩下的不多，好像人打橄榄树―在尽上的枝梢上只剩两三个果子；在多果树的旁枝上只剩四五个果子。这是耶和华―以色列的　神说的。
verses.en: There will be some left behind,as when an olive tree is beaten—two or three ripe olives remain toward the very top,four or five on its fruitful branches,”says the Lord God of Israel.

verses.zh: 当那日，人必仰望造他们的主，眼目重看以色列的圣者。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] men will trust in their Creator;[NOTE:2] they will depend on[NOTE:3] the Holy One of Israel.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “in that day” (so ASV, NASB, NIV); KJV “At that day.”
Heb “man will gaze toward his maker.”
Heb “his eyes will look toward.”
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.

verses.zh: 他们必不仰望祭坛，就是自己手所筑的，也不重看自己指头所做的，无论是木偶是日像。
verses.en: They will no longer trust in[NOTE:1] the altars their hands made,or depend on the Asherah poles and incense altars their fingers made.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “he will not gaze toward.”
Heb “and that which his fingers made he will not see, the Asherah poles and the incense altars.”

verses.zh: 在那日，他们的坚固城必像树林中和山顶上所撇弃的地方，就是从前在以色列人面前被人撇弃的。这样，地就荒凉了。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] their fortified cities will be like the abandoned summits of the Amorites,[NOTE:2] which they abandoned because of the Israelites;there will be desolation.
notes: Heb “in that day” (so KJV).

The Hebrew text reads literally, “like the abandonment of the wooded height and the top one.” The following relative clause appears to allude back to the Israelite conquest of the land, so it seems preferable to emend הַחֹרֶשׁ וְהָאָמִיר (hakhoresh vehaʾamir, “the wooded height and the top one”) to חֹרֵשֵׁי הָאֱמֹרִי (khoreshe haʾemori, “[like the abandonment] of the wooded heights of the Amorites”).

verses.zh: 因你忘记救你的　神，不记念你能力的磐石；所以，你栽上佳美的树秧子，插上异样的栽子。
verses.en: For you ignore[NOTE:1] the God who rescues you;you pay no attention to your strong protector.[NOTE:2] So this is what happens:You cultivate beautiful plantsand plant exotic vines.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “you have forgotten” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “and the rocky cliff of your strength you do not remember.”

Heb “a vine, a strange one.” The substantival adjective זָר (zar) functions here as an appositional genitive. It could refer to a cultic plant of some type, associated with a pagan rite. But it is more likely that it refers to an exotic, or imported, type of vine, one that is foreign (i.e., “strange”) to Israel.

verses.zh: 栽种的日子，你周围圈上篱笆，又到早晨使你所种的开花；但在愁苦极其伤痛的日子，所收割的都飞去了。
verses.en: The day you begin cultivating, you do what you can to make it grow;[NOTE:1] the morning you begin planting, you do what you can to make it sprout.Yet the harvest will disappear[NOTE:2] in the day of diseaseand incurable pain.
notes: Heb “in the day of your planting you [?].” The precise meaning of the verb תְּשַׂגְשֵׂגִי (tesagsegi) is unclear. It is sometimes derived from שׂוּג/סוּג (sug, “to fence in”; see BDB 691 s.v. II סוּג). In this case one could translate “you build a protective fence.” However, the parallelism is tighter if one derives the form from שָׂגָא/שָׂגָה (sagaʾ/sagah, “to grow”); see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:351, n. 4. For this verb, see BDB 960 s.v. שָׂגָא.

The Hebrew text has, “a heap of harvest.” However, better sense is achieved if נֵד (ned, “heap”) is emended to a verb. Options include נַד (nad, Qal perfect third masculine singular from נָדַד [nadad, “flee, depart”]), נָדַד (Qal perfect third masculine singular from נָדַד), נֹדֵד (noded, Qal active participle from נָדַד), and נָד (nad, Qal perfect third masculine singular, or participle masculine singular, from נוּד [nud, “wander, flutter”]). See BDB 626 s.v. נוּד and HALOT 672 s.v. I נדד. One could translate literally: “[the harvest] departs,” or “[the harvest] flies away.”

verses.zh: 唉！多民哄嚷，好像海浪匉訇；列邦奔腾，好像猛水滔滔；
verses.en: Beware, you many nations massing together,[NOTE:1] those who make a commotion as loud as the roaring of the sea’s waves.[NOTE:2] Beware, you people making such an uproar,[NOTE:3] those who make an uproar as loud as the roaring of powerful waves.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] the massing of the many nations.”
Heb “like the loud noise of the seas, they make a loud noise.”
Heb “the uproar of the peoples.”
Heb “like the uproar of mighty waters they are in an uproar.”

verses.zh: 列邦奔腾，好像多水滔滔；但　神斥责他们，他们就远远逃避，又被追赶，如同山上的风前糠，又如暴风前的旋风土。
verses.en: Though these people make an uproar as loud as the roaring of powerful waves,[NOTE:1] when he shouts at[NOTE:2] them, they will flee to a distant land,driven before the wind like dead weeds on the hillsor like dead thistles[NOTE:3] before a strong gale.
notes: Heb “the peoples are in an uproar like the uproar of mighty waters.”

Or “rebukes.” The verb and related noun are used in theophanies of God’s battle cry, which terrifies his enemies. See, for example, Pss 18:15; 76:7; 106:9; Isa 50:2; Nah 1:4, and A. Caquot, TDOT 3:49-53.
Or perhaps “tumbleweed” (NAB, NIV, CEV); KJV “like a rolling thing.”

verses.zh: 到晚上有惊吓，未到早晨他们就没有了。这是掳掠我们之人所得的分，是抢夺我们之人的报应。
verses.en: In the evening there is sudden terror;[NOTE:1] by morning they vanish.[NOTE:2] This is the fate of those who try to plunder us,the destiny of those who try to loot us![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “at the time of evening, look, sudden terror.”
Heb “before morning he is not.”
Heb “this is the portion of those who plunder us, and the lot of those who loot us.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ISAIAH 17

- This context reflects the consequences of the alliance between Syria and Israel to rebel against
Assyria. It is often called the Syro-Ephramatic War (735 B.C.)

- Syria and Israel tried to get Judah to join their coalition (cf. Isa. 7:1-8:23), but Ahaz refused and
asked Assyria for help.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 17:1-3

1The oracle concerning Damascus.

"Behold, Damascus is about to be removed from being a city

And will become a fallen ruin.

2The cities of Aroer are forsaken;

They will be for flocks to lie down in,

And there will be no one to frighten them.

3The fortified city will disappear from Ephraim,

And sovereignty from Damascus

And the remnant of Aram;

They will be like the glory of the sons of Israel,"

Declares the Lord of hosts.

17:1 "Damascus" This was the capital of Aram/Syria. The invasion and destruction of Syria have
been alluded to earlier in Isa. 7:16; 8:4; 10:9. It was an ancient city (cf. Gen. 14:15; 15:2) and an
important city located on the northern and northeastern trade routes.

▣ Notice the synonymous parallelism of lines 2 and 3. Tiglath-pileser III partially destroyed
Damascus in 732 B.C. It was rebuilt as a regional Assyrian capital. Remember
all prophecy is hyperbolic (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of
Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 99-102, and G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 110-117).

17:2 "The cities of Aroer" This phrase is confusing.

- This is the name of a city, not a region.

- There are several cities that go by this name (BDB 792, which may refer to a "tree" or a
"mountain crest," AB, vol. 1, p. 399). Three of the four possible sites are south of Syrian territory.

- The LXX leaves out the place name (as does REB).

- The Peshitta spells it Adoer.

It seems that Syria and Israel are linked together in this chapter. They had formed a
political/military alliance against Assyria and tried to make Judah join. This co-alliance caused the
Syro-Ephraimite war where these two northern nations invaded Judah (cf. Isa. 7:16; 8:4; 10:9) to force
her to join their fight against Assyria.

Most of the references are to the Northern Ten Tribes called

- Israel/Jacob (Isa. 17:4)

- Samaria

- Ephraim (Isa. 17:3)

Syria was under Israelite control during the United Monarchy period.

Aroer is probably a reference to the fortress located on the Arnon River near Dibon.

17:3 The walled fortified cities of Syria and Ephraim will disappear (BDB 991, KB 1407,
Niphal perfect with waw). The JPSOA has a footnote that
supports a textual emendation from "Ephraim" (BDB 68)
אפרים to
ארם "Aram" (BDB 78), which would be a true parallelism.
But if the first strophe is about the Syro-Ephraimite War, then the parallelism is already there.
I think Isa. 17:3 has an AB, BA poetic pattern (chiasim), as it is in the MT.

▣ "the remnant of Aram" This phrase could refer to

- the capital as the only place of Syrian power that remains (and it will fall, Isa. 17:6)

- when the capital falls most of the population will not survive

▣ Although the last two lines of Isa. 17:3 appear to be positive, they are not. Ephraim is
destroyed in 3a, now Syria shares her fate (sarcastically, "glory," cf. Isa. 17:4). "Glory" could refer
to the capital of Israel, "Samaria," which fell after an extended siege to Assyria under Sargon II
in 722 B.C.

▣ "Declares the Lord of hosts" YHWH is in control of history,
especially those events that affect His covenant people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 17:4-11

4Now in that day the glory of Jacob will fade,

And the fatness of his flesh will become lean.

5It will be even like the reaper gathering the standing grain,

As his arm harvests the ears,

Or it will be like one gleaning ears of grain

In the valley of Rephaim.

6Yet gleanings will be left in it like the shaking of an olive tree,

Two or three olives on the topmost bough,

Four or five on the branches of a fruitful tree,

Declares the Lord, the God of Israel.

7In that day man will have regard for his Maker

And his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel.

8He will not have regard for the altars, the work of his hands,

Nor will he look to that which his fingers have made,

Even the Asherim and incense stands.

9In that day their strong cities will be like forsaken places in the forest,

Or like branches which they abandoned before the sons of Israel;

And the land will be a desolation.

10For you have forgotten the God of your salvation

And have not remembered the rock of your refuge.

Therefore you plant delightful plants

And set them with vine slips of a strange god.

11In the day that you plant it you carefully fence it in,

And in the morning you bring your seed to blossom;

But the harvest will be a heap

In a day of sickliness and incurable pain.

17:4 "in that day" It is uncertain how the text which follows should be divided into poetic strophes.
This phrase could denote the start of a new strophe (cf. Isa. 17:4, Isa. 17:7, Isa. 17:9, Isa. 17:11). It
is difficult to know the difference between poetry and elevated prose (note paragraph divisions and poetic
lines of different translations at the beginning of the chapter).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣

NASB
"fade"

NKJV, REB, Peshitta
"wane"

NRSV
"brought low"

TEV
"come to an end"

NJB
"dimimish"

JPSOA
"dwindle"

LXX
"failing"

This VERB (BDB 195, KB 223, Niphal
IMPERFECT) originally referred to low hanging fruit or limbs, but
the Niphal stem denoted that which was brought low or laid low (cf. Jdg. 6:6). The Qal
stem is used in Isa. 19:6 and 38:14.

This is the first of several negative statements describing the fate of the Northern Ten Tribes.

- glory. . .will fade, Isa. 17:4

- fatness of his flesh will become lean, Isa. 17:4

- Jacob/Israel will be cut down, Isa. 17:5

- only a few olives left at the very top, Isa. 17:6

17:5 "the valley of Rephaim" This refers to a fertile valley southwest of Jerusalem which is
mentioned several times in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 5:18,22; 23:13; 1 Chr. 11:15; 14:9; and here). It must
have served as the origin of Isaiah's imagery of expected fruitfulness thwarted (cf. Isa. 17:4). Why
Isaiah used a site in Judah, not Israel, is uncertain. "Rephaim" is the name used for a group of tall Canaanites.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

17:6 The initial harvest of olive trees was by shaking or striking the tree (cf. Isa. 24:13;
Deut. 24:20). There were always a few olives left that would not fall. These were usually left for the
poor (i.e. gleaners). Isaiah uses them as a symbol for a remnant of survivors.

▣ "Two or three. . .Four or five" This is an example of a Hebrew idiom for an
indefinite amount.

17:7-8 These verses form a contrast. Isaiah 17:7 denotes repentance, Isa. 17:8 what they turn
from (i.e. idolatry). The question is to whom are these two verses directed.

- Israel

- Israel and Syria

- Israel, Syria, and Assyria

- all ANE cultures (i.e. "men," האדם)

Is this meant to be parallel to Isa. 7, 9, and 11? Also notice the promised victory of God's
people in Isa. 17:12-14 (esp. 14d)!

17:7 The parallelism of the verse links "Maker" (i.e. the Creator of heaven and earth or the creator
of Israel, cf. Isa. 51:13) with "the Holy One of Israel" (a title used almost exclusively by Isaiah). This
is an allusion to monotheism!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

17:8 Instead of YHWH being the "maker" they have made their own gods (i.e. Ba'als
and Asherim, line 3; 2:8,20; 30:22; 31:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "incense stands" The term (BDB 329 calls it a "sun-pillar," but KB 329 calls it a transportable
"incense-altar"). It is always used in a negative sense in the context of idol worship (cf. Lev. 26:30;
2 Chr. 14:5; 34:4,7; Isa. 17:8; 27:9; Ezek. 6:4,6).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 903, suggests that it may refer to the sanctuary of a foreign god.

17:9 This seems to begin a new thought unit. It describes the coming judgment in hyperbolic agricultural
imagery (MT)

- like the forsaken places of the forest

- like branches which they abandoned

- the land will be a desolation

This verse is translated very differently by the Septuagint and its translation is followed
by JB, NRSV, and REB (and the JPSOA seems to acknowledge its validity in its footnote). The phrase denotes

- a rapid exodus where useless things are abandoned

- people groups conquered by the Israelites in the Conquest (i.e. the Amorites and Hivites)

- relating to Israel's past victories during the Conquest (i.e. Joshua)

(NRSV, LXX, NET)

- relating to Assyria's invasion and destruction

17:10 This verse is uniquely addressed to Israel and the reason for their judgment by their covenant Deity.

- forgotten the God (Eloah, BDB 43) of your salvation (i.e. Ps. 78:11,42; see note below)

- not remembered the rock of your refuge (i.e. Ps. 18:1-3; 78:35)

- planted delightful plants in honor of a strange god (cf. Isa. 1:29-30; 65:3; 66:17, i.e. sacred gardens
or trees. It may refer to Adonis/Tammuz, a vegetation god to whom flowers were planted early
in the spring, cf. AB, vol. 6, p. 318)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

▣ "the God of your salvation" This is a recurrent description of Israel's God (cf. Isa. 12:2;
17:10; 33:2; 45:17; 61:16; 62:10; Ps. 65:5; 68:19; 85:4). Salvation denotes deliverance from any force or
pressure that denies or cancels YHWH's covenant desire for His people. Only Israel's sin can thwart His
desires for them and yet, He remains "the God of your salvation" (cf. Micah 7:7; Hab. 3:13,18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT term)

17:11 This refers to the sacred gardens #3 in Isa. 17:10 above.

- they plant it carefully

- they fence it

- they fertilize it

It will grow and reproduce amazingly fast, but will result in

- harvest a heap

- sickliness

- incurable pain (cf. Job 34:6; Jer. 15:18; 17:9; 30:12,15; Micah 1:9)

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 17:12-14

12Alas, the uproar of many peoples

Who roar like the roaring of the seas,

And the rumbling of nations

Who rush on like the rumbling of mighty waters!

13The nations rumble on like the rumbling of many waters,

But He will rebuke them and they will flee far away,

And be chased like chaff in the mountains before the wind,

Or like whirling dust before a gale.

14At evening time, behold, there is terror!

Before morning they are no more.

Such will be the portion of those who plunder us

And the lot of those who pillage us.

17:12-14 The strophe of invasion and destruction could refer to

- the Assyrian army defeating and destroying much of Syria and Israel

- the Syrian and Israelite armies approaching Jerusalem to force Judah into joining their rebellion against Assyria

This is the final strophe of chapter 17. It is characterized by parallelism and the repeated
use of two roots.

- BDB 242, KB 250, "murmur," "grown," "roar," or "be boisterous"

- NOUN, Isa. 17:12

- Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, Isa. 17:12

- Qal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:12

- BDB 980, KB 1367, "roar," "uproar," "din," or "crash"

- NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:12

- NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:12

- Niphal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:12

- NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:13

- Niphal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:13

- parallel imagery, Isa. 17:13

- like chaff, Isa. 17:13

- like dust, Isa. 17:13

YHWH's roar is louder than the tumult of the nations and they will retreat as a result! He overcomes
the chaotic waters again as in creation (cf. Psalm 29. see

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS).

- contrast, Isa. 17:14

- at evening, behold there is terror

- before morning they are no more

- synonyms, Isa. 17:14

- plunder, BDB 1042, KB 1367, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE

- pillage, BDB 102, KB 117, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE

17:14 "Before morning they are no more" This phrase has no VERBAL, which
in Hebrew, would denote emphasis. This line gives a restorative context to Isa. 17:12-14. This strophe is parallel
to the thoughts of Psalm 2. YHWH sends the nations (i.e. to punish His people for their covenant disobedience
and lack of faithfulness), but He judges the very same nations. His people are safe in Him! This reversal
is similar to Isa. 10:33-34.

Often in Isaiah God's deliverance is connected to the coming of light (cf. Isa. 8:22-9:2; 17:14;
29:18; 30:26; 33:2; 42:16; 49:9-10; 58:8,10; 60:1-3,19-20).

▣ "the portion" This term (BDB 324) denotes God's will in the imagery of a divine lot cast. It
does not mean an arbitrary destiny or fate, but events are in the hand of God (cf. Jer. 13:25).
